summary: Defines four ciphers based on RC5 in enough detail for different implementations to interoperate: RC5, RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad, and RC5-CTS. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes a scrambling machine and several ways to use it, so everyone's machines produce the same result.

questions: how many rounds should rc5 use
subtitle: A precise description of the RC5 block cipher and three ways to use it, so different implementations produce identical output.

tldr.problem: Implementations of the RC5 cipher and its common modes need a single detailed description, or their encrypted output will not match.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the RC5 block cipher (key expansion plus a round function of additions, XORs and rotations) and three modes on top of it: RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad and RC5-CTS. It supplies C sample code, a test program and test vectors.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational restatement of existing material, not a standard. The security section suggests at least 12 rounds for the 64-bit block version and a 128-bit key.

facts.label: Block size
facts.value: Twice the word size (64 bits for 32-bit words)

today: RFC 2040 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it specifies no Internet standard.

sections.title: Four Ciphers in One Memo
sections.content:
The memo defines four ciphers in enough detail for different implementations to interoperate. RC5 is the raw block cipher: it turns a fixed-size input block into a fixed-size output block using a key. RC5-CBC is Cipher Block Chaining mode and handles messages whose length is a multiple of the block size. RC5-CBC-Pad handles any length, with ciphertext at most one block longer than the plaintext. RC5-CTS is Cipher Text Stealing mode, which handles any length and keeps the ciphertext the same length as the plaintext.

RC5 was invented by Ronald L. Rivest of MIT in 1994 and is parameterized by block size, number of rounds and key length. The memo calls itself a restatement of existing published material and says only encryption is described, since decryption inverts the steps. It also notes that RSA Data Security had filed a patent application on RC5 and sought trademark protection for the names.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one basic scrambler and three ways to use it on long messages, depending on whether the message fits neatly into chunks.

sections.title: Parameters and Key Expansion
sections.content:
The word size W is half the block size: 32-bit words give a 64-bit block, and the memo covers word sizes 32 and 64. The number of rounds is R (0 to 255), the secret key K is b bytes long (0 to 255), and the expanded key table S holds T = 2*(R + 1) words.

Key expansion works in three steps. First the key bytes are copied into an array L of words. Then S is filled with a fixed pattern built from two constants, Pw and Qw, derived from e and the golden ratio. Finally the key is mixed in: the loop runs three times the larger of the size of L and T, updating S and L with additions and left rotations. For W = 32 the constants are 0xb7e15163 and 0x9e3779b9.
sections.plainLanguage: Before scrambling, the machine stirs your secret key into a long list of numbers, like mixing a spoonful of dye into a big bucket of paint.

sections.title: The RC5 Block Cipher
sections.content:
A block is loaded as two words, A and B, least significant byte first. The first two words of S are added to them. Then the round function repeats R times: A is XORed with B, rotated left by an amount taken from B, and the next unused word of S is added. The second half does the same with the roles of A and B swapped.

Only the low-order bits of the rotation word matter (log base 2 of W bits). Finally A and B are written back out as bytes. The memo describes this version as the original RC5, version number 16 in decimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers take turns stirring each other with a twist, over and over. The more times they stir, the harder it is to guess what you started with.

sections.title: CBC, CBC-Pad and CTS Modes
sections.content:
In CBC mode each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before it is encrypted. The first block is XORed with an initialization vector (IV), one block long. The memo uses an Init, Update, Final pattern: Update processes parts of a message, and Final handles whatever is left.

For RC5-CBC, Final only checks that the length was a multiple of the block size. For RC5-CBC-Pad, Final adds between one and BB padding bytes, each holding the number of padding bytes (eight bytes of padding are all 0x08).

For RC5-CTS, CBC is used for all but the last two portions of plaintext. The final partial block is handled by encrypting the second-to-last block, borrowing its leading bytes as the last ciphertext block, and encrypting once more, so the output length equals the input length.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk is mixed with the scrambled chunk before it, so the same words look different each time. Padding fills the last box so it is full; ciphertext stealing borrows from the neighbor so no filler is needed.

sections.title: Security Guidance
sections.content:
The memo says RC5 was relatively new and still under review. Early results suggest that for the 64-bit block version, 12 rounds will suffice to resist linear and differential cryptanalysis, and that 16 rounds is an appropriate minimum for the 128-bit block version. Block sizes below 64 bits should not be used for cryptographic security.

A key length of 128 bits is described as adequate against brute force by a well funded opponent for a couple of decades. For export-limited 40-bit keys, the memo warns against simply using a 5-byte key and suggests hashing a 128-bit seed with MD5. For high-security use, the key of a 64-bit block cipher should change after 2**32 blocks.

Section 11 gives ASN.1 identifiers for RC5-CBC and RC5-CBC-Pad, with parameters for version, rounds (8..127), block size in bits (64 or 128) and an optional IV.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer secret and more stirring make the lock harder to pick, and you should swap keys now and then rather than using one forever.
